title: Mechawanienck (New Utrecht)
summary: Mechawanienck is a locality in Kings County. The name appears in a New Utrecht deed describing land running from Gouwanis across the hills toward the southeast side of Amersfoort, or Flatlands.
why_this_matters: The name may preserve a Lenape route across Brooklyn’s hills that was already old when the 1652 deed was written.
introduction_content: Mechawanienck appears only once in early records, in the New Utrecht deed of November 22, 1652. William Wallace Tooker read the name as an “old Indian trail or path.”
history_content:
An old path across the hills

The deed describes land “stretching from behind Mr. Paulus’ land, called Gouwanis, across the hills to Mechawanienck lying on the south east side Amersfoort (Flatlands) and thence past Gravesend to the sea following the marks on the trees.”

Tooker found no other early mention of the place. He derived the name from mechowi, “old” or “ancient, old in use,” and a word for a road or path, giving “the old path or trail.” If he is right, the name marked a route that was already old in 1652, one of the paths that crossed Brooklyn’s hills.

William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent (1911), printed pp. 123–124, citing Colonial History of New York, vol. XIV, p. 190.

The same 1652 agreements included a demand that Nayack residents leave; see Brooklyn’s colonial land claims. The ridge these paths crossed runs through Prospect Park.
translation_content:
The name is interpreted as the old path or trail, from language connected with old or ancient use and a road, walking road, or path.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place names are variously expressions of identity, power, location, and culture.”

— Molly Williamson, Historical geographies of place naming: Colonial practices and beyond (2023), section 3, opening sentence

The name may preserve a Lenape route across Brooklyn’s hills that was already old when the 1652 deed was written.
whereintheworld_content: Map location note: the pin is placed in the Flatlands/New Utrecht boundary landscape of Brooklyn to represent the deed locality; it is not an exact historic trail or boundary point.
